name: ProofOfKeags
cooked:
Originally published on my site. Replicating here because I think the Delving audience has an interest in this work.

From the project’s inception until now, btc-verified has been focused on building up, layer by layer, a very minimal model of consensus. Last month’s post talked about how we can discover hidden subtleties in how something works when we try to formalize it. However, even as we formalize things we have to resist the temptation to merely assume that the precise map we have created actually reflects the reality on the ground. This month, however, I decided to take a stab at anchoring this model to the Bitcoin network as it exists in the real world.

It’s tricky to do this type of thing because it forces us to ask the question how do we know the map matches the territory? How close can we get?

For most software that you want to verify it is an option on the table to simply write the software in a verifiable language, compile that down to code that actually runs on silicon and be on your merry way. Alternatively, if the code you’re trying to verify is pure C code, there are ways to verify the C code directly since C’s operational semantics are small enough to reason somewhat efficiently about.

The problem here is that Bitcoin Core, which on a practical level defines the Bitcoin protocol, is neither written in a verifiable language, nor is it written in pure C. Rather, it is written in modern C++ so verifying it directly, while possible on theoretical grounds is very far out of reach with my current resources.

So what can we do instead?

The main thing we are trying to establish is that our model does not differ from Bitcoin Core in any observable way with respect to its protocol semantics. Hypothetically, if we were able to come up with an implementation of the protocol in Lean that had no differences in behavior from Bitcoin Core, it would mean that the model, in a sense, IS Bitcoin Core. If the model predicts reality with 100% accuracy, we can say that the model is “correct”.

This seems like a simple enough thesis, but it is far from well defined enough to build something around. What constitutes a behavior? How can we observe the behavior? How can we tell if it’s different or not? What things are implementation details and what things are essential semantics?

People have been trying for years to extract out Bitcoin consensus from the rest of Bitcoin Core and the most recent label for this effort is the libbitcoinkernel project. This carves out a chunk of Core inside of which is the consensus verification code and outside of which we can safely write all kinds of custom implementation experiments without compromising the safety of consensus. The original purpose of this project is actually to reduce the usage of non-Core implementations of consensus. However, it also gives us a natural entry point for our purposes here.

To do this carve out, libbitcoinkernel must define an interface that preserves the essential invariants of consensus and for it to be usable, its interface must give us the ability to know whether something is consensus valid or not.

What I have decided to do is to take advantage of the existence of this interface and ensure that btc-verified can serve as the implementation behind it. We are not doing this to encourage people to run btc-verified’s consensus instead of Bitcoin Core’s. We are doing this to set up a benchmark of btc-verified’s faithfulness of matching Core’s behavior on the faultline that has already been drawn by the Bitcoin Core team.

Once we have established a trivial implementation of libbitcoinkernel’s interface in the btc-verified project, then we can take advantage of another technique that has an established practice in the space: differential fuzzing.

bitcoinfuzz is a project whose aim is differential fuzzing of different bitcoin implementations. The idea here is that we spew entropy at the kernel interface and ensure that for any given payload that Core’s kernel and btc-verified’s kernel report the same result, including any state changes that are made by the operation executed.

bitcoinfuzz already has an established track record and has found numerous bugs in different implementations using this strategy. Indeed, short of proofs, the best we can do to establish equality is to do high-entropy sampling of the behavior of each implementation and ensure they never diverge.

Of course, you never know if the next sample you take is the one that reveals a difference. This is the exact reason that formal verification even has a place, because you cannot establish universal laws through sampling alone, but it does have a practical benefit of reducing the probability of divergent behavior the more that the sample space saturates the control flow graph.

Following this thread, I put together a standalone differential fuzzing harness for Bitcoin Core and btc-verified, specifically against the kernel interface, and we have nine of the kernel functions backed by a Lean implementation. These functions cover transaction creation, copying, serialization, checking, and the associated validation-state objects. The harness is built directly on libFuzzer. It gives the same transaction bytes to Core and btc-verified, then compares their observable behavior.

As of right now btc-verified does not implement the entire kernel interface even trivially, but it does implement a subset of it with apparently correct semantics for the following behaviors:

  • Parsing: Given identical bytes, do both implementations accept them as a transaction object? This is distinct from accepting the transaction as valid.
  • Serialization: For accepted inputs, do both report the same serialization status and produce exactly the same bytes?
  • Transaction-local checking: Do they agree on the verdict for rules concerning input/output presence, duplicate or null input references, output-value and stripped-size limits, and the special coinbase conditions? These checks don’t consult the UTXO set or execute scripts.
  • Reported validation state: Do they return the same validation mode and result category, beyond merely agreeing on acceptance or rejection?
  • State reuse: After checking a known-invalid transaction, does checking the next transaction replace that previous result consistently—including clearing the invalid state when the next transaction passes?

As of this writing these behaviors are identical between btc-verified and Bitcoin Core when observed over this battery:

  • 100,000 fuzz executions: this measures how many attempts for disagreement were made. Each execution feeds one byte sequence into the differential harness, which runs both implementations and compares their observations. This measures testing volume. It doesn’t count unique transactions: inputs can repeat, and malformed inputs may be rejected during parsing without reaching transaction checking. Mutations are also related to earlier inputs, rather than independent random samples.
  • 11 regression inputs: this measures how many pre-determined cases are explicitly replayed. These ensure particular cases are checked every time, regardless of what mutation happens to discover. “Regression” here doesn’t mean each input previously exposed a bug. The ones here include real legacy and SegWit transactions, malformed encodings, a transaction that parses but fails checking, and three transactions immediately below, at, and above the million-byte stripped-size boundary. Those large cases matter because the mutation campaign’s 4,096-byte limit prevents it from discovering them.
  • 264 retained corpus inputs: this was the size of the working corpus at the end of the October 18 CI run. LibFuzzer keeps inputs that contribute useful coverage feedback and uses them as starting points for further mutations. The final corpus count describes that working collection, including retained starting seeds.

This differential test additionally runs as a CI check before new code is merged allowing observed disagreement with Core to block changes to the code.

There is a ton of work still to do to strengthen the link between btc-verified and Bitcoin Core but assuming we can establish a credible link between them it allows us to borrow some of the theorems and findings we can establish natively in btc-verified and use them to make statements about Bitcoin Core’s behavior.

Over the coming month the plan is to push forwards on filling out the rest of the kernel interface so we can officially connect this map to this territory, at least tenuously for now, before pushing forwards on analyzing the map itself.
